  waiting for something to finish. The bees were still coming and going around him. The postman did not know what to do,
  so he went and fetched Ivo from the other end of the village, where Ivo was working as a joiner, and Ivo came running
  with sawdust still in his hair.

  After the funeral, which was small and cold and attended mostly by people who had bought honey from Josef for twenty
  years, Ivo stood in the orchard and looked at the twelve white boxes in their neat row. He did not know what to do
  with them. He had not kept bees since he was a boy, and then only the single hive, and only in the summers, when his
  father had been short-handed and needed someone to fetch things. He knew the names of the parts. He could not remember
  how to tell whether a colony was queenless, or what a swarm cell looked like, or when the honey was ready to take.

  His sister Hana wanted to sell the hives. She lived in the city now, in a flat above a bakery, and she had no interest
  in bees or orchards or the smell of smoke. She had come back for the funeral with a grey coat and a list of things to
  be done, and she had made it clear that the house would be sold in the autumn and the orchard would be cleared and
  the land would be turned into something useful.

  "You can't keep them," she said, standing at the gate with her arms folded against the wind. "You don't even know
  how."

  "I know some of it."

  "Some of it isn't enough, Ivo. They'll die. You'll feel terrible. Then we'll have to pay someone to come and take them
  away, and that's money."
